title: Make Cord Clutter a Thing of the Past With This Powerful Wireless HDMI Streamer
gist: A hands-on WIRED review rates the $250 Nyrius Phoenix Home True 4K60 wireless HDMI transmitter 8/10, finding lag-free 4K60 streaming up to 500 feet and remote computer control via USB-C, undercutting pricier competitors like the $450 SIIG extender on range.

insights.claim: The Nyrius Phoenix Home True 4K60 wireless HDMI transmitter/receiver kit costs $250 and transmits lossless 4K video at up to 60 frames per second with Dolby Atmos, DTS, and 7.1 surround sound support.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Establishes the price-performance bar in the consumer wireless-HDMI category.
insights.locator: The transmission quality is frankly amazing

insights.claim: The Phoenix Home can transmit up to 500 feet in open areas and 75 feet through walls, floors, and ceilings, a longer range than the pricier $450 SIIG 4K HDMI Wireless Extender Kit.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: A cheaper product beating a more expensive competitor on range is a competitive signal worth tracking in the niche wireless-AV accessory market.
insights.locator: That's a better range than the more expensive options like the $450 SIIG

insights.claim: The manufacturer states the system has up to 88 milliseconds of latency, but the reviewer did not notice any lag across gaming, Blu-ray playback, and remote laptop use.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Sub-100ms latency appears sufficient for consumer gaming and video use cases, a relevant benchmark for wireless-AV product positioning.
insights.locator: The brand says there is a system latency of up to 88 milliseconds

insights.claim: A USB-C port on the transmitter lets a user connect a laptop and control it remotely via a keyboard and mouse plugged into the receiver, extending the product beyond simple video streaming into remote-desktop-style use.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Feature creep toward general-purpose wireless KVM functionality could widen the addressable use cases (e.g., classroom AV) beyond home theater.
insights.locator: The Phoenix Home transmitter also has a USB-C port

insights.claim: Both the transmitter and receiver units ran noticeably hot after a full day of continuous use, noted as the reviewer's main complaint.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: A minor thermal design issue that could affect long-term reliability or become a competitive weak point versus rivals.
insights.locator: My only gripe—and a minor one at that

insights.claim: Testing with an old Sony Bravia television produced a strange noise, which a Nyrius representative attributed to an HDMI handshake failure with older TV hardware.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Compatibility gaps with legacy hardware are a recurring risk for wireless-AV products marketed to broad consumer audiences.
insights.locator: The only glitch I experienced was that the Google TV streamer emitted a strange noise

insights.claim: The review opens by citing a 2010 UCLA study that found an association between household clutter and elevated cortisol (stress hormone) levels, used to frame cable clutter as a real wellness problem the product solves.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Shows how consumer-electronics marketing increasingly leans on wellness/stress framing rather than pure specs to justify purchases.
insights.locator: A famous 2010 study from UCLA found an association between household clutter and elevated cortisol levels
